prompt: Does the open() function set the file offset to the beginning of the file when a new file descriptor is created?
target: Yes. "The file offset used to mark the current position within the file shall be set to the beginning of the file." This clause explicitly mandates that the initial position for any new open file description is the start of the file. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 open() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: Does the open() function fail if the named file is a directory and the oflag includes O_WRONLY?
target: Yes. "The named file is a directory and oflag includes O_WRONLY or O_RDWR, or includes O_CREAT without O_DIRECTORY." This clause explicitly defines the condition where the file is a directory and the open flags include O_WRONLY, causing the function to fail with the [EISDIR] error. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 open() section ERRORS

prompt: Does the close() function remove all outstanding record locks owned by the process on the file associated with the file descriptor?
target: Yes. "All outstanding record locks owned by the process on the file associated with the file descriptor shall be removed (that is, unlocked)." This clause explicitly mandates that the function unlocks all record locks held by the process when the file descriptor is deallocated. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 close() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: Does the close() function fail if the fildes argument is not an open file descriptor?
target: Yes. "The fildes argument is not a open file descriptor." This clause explicitly defines the condition under which the function shall fail with the [EBADF] error. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 close() section ERRORS

prompt: What happens if a read() is interrupted by a signal before it reads any data?
target: Yes, it returns -1 with errno set to [EINTR]. "If a read() is interrupted by a signal before it reads any data, it shall return -1 with errno set to [EINTR]." This means the function stops immediately and signals the interruption via the error code. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 read() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: Under what conditions does the read() function fail with the EAGAIN error for a socket?
target: Yes, the read() function fails with EAGAIN for a socket when the file is a socket, the O_NONBLOCK flag is set for the file descriptor, and the thread would be delayed in the read operation. "[EAGAIN] or [EWOULDBLOCK] The file is a socket, the O_NONBLOCK flag is set for the file descriptor, and the thread would be delayed in the read operation." This means that if a non-blocking socket read cannot immediately return data without waiting, the function returns this error to indicate the operation would block. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 read() section ERRORS

prompt: What happens to the file offset after a successful write() to a regular file?
target: Yes, the file offset is incremented by the number of bytes actually written. "Before successful return from write(), the file offset shall be incremented by the number of bytes actually written." This means that once the write operation completes successfully, the position in the file moves forward by the exact amount of data that was written. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 write() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: Under what conditions does the write() function fail with the EPIPE error for a socket?
target: Yes, the write() function fails with EPIPE when a write is attempted on a socket that is shut down for writing or is no longer connected. "A write was attempted on a socket that is shut down for writing, or is no longer connected. In the latter case, if the socket is of type SOCK_STREAM, a SIGPIPE signal shall also be sent to the thread." This clause explicitly defines the socket-specific scenarios for this error, including the additional signal requirement for stream sockets. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 write() section ERRORS

prompt: Does the lseek() function extend the size of a file by itself?
target: No. "The lseek() function shall not, by itself, extend the size of a file." This means that while the file offset can be moved beyond the current end of data, the actual file size remains unchanged until new data is written. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 lseek() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: Does the lseek() function fail if the fildes argument is associated with a pipe?
target: Yes. "The fildes argument is associated with a pipe, FIFO, or socket." This clause explicitly lists a pipe as a condition under which the function shall fail. Therefore, if the file descriptor refers to a pipe, lseek() will return an error. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 lseek() section ERRORS

prompt: What happens to the FD_CLOEXEC flag associated with fildes2 if fildes is equal to fildes2?
target: No, the flag is not changed. "If fildes is equal to fildes2, the FD_CLOEXEC flag associated with fildes2 shall not be changed." This means that when the source and target descriptors are identical, the existing close-on-exec status remains untouched. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 dup() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: Under what condition does the dup2() function fail if the argument fildes2 is negative or greater than or equal to {OPEN_MAX}?
target: Yes, the dup2() function shall fail if the argument fildes2 is negative or greater than or equal to {OPEN_MAX}. "The fildes argument is not a valid open file descriptor or the argument fildes2 is negative or greater than or equal to {OPEN_MAX}." This means that if fildes2 falls outside the valid range, the function returns an error. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 dup() section ERRORS

prompt: What happens to the FD_CLOEXEC flag associated with fildes2 if fildes is equal to fildes2?
target: No, the flag is not changed. "If fildes is equal to fildes2, the FD_CLOEXEC flag associated with fildes2 shall not be changed." This means the existing state of the flag remains intact without being cleared or modified. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 dup2() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: Under what condition does the dup2() function fail if the argument fildes2 is negative or greater than or equal to {OPEN_MAX}?
target: Yes, the dup2() function shall fail if "The fildes argument is not a valid open file descriptor or the argument fildes2 is negative or greater than or equal to {OPEN_MAX}." This specific condition is listed under the [EBADF] error code for the dup2() function. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 dup2() section ERRORS

prompt: Does the F_SETLKW command cause the thread to wait if a shared or exclusive lock is blocked by other locks?
target: Yes. "This command shall be equivalent to F_SETLK except that if a shared or exclusive lock is blocked by other locks, the thread shall wait until the request can be satisfied." This explicitly states that the waiting behavior occurs when the lock is blocked by other locks, distinguishing it from the immediate return of F_SETLK. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 fcntl() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: Under what condition does the fcntl() function fail with the [EDEADLK] error?
target: Yes, the fcntl() function fails with [EDEADLK] when the command is F_SETLKW, the lock is blocked by another process, and waiting for the lock would cause a deadlock. "The cmd argument is F_SETLKW, the lock is blocked by a lock from another process, and putting the calling process to sleep to wait for that lock to become free would cause a deadlock." This means the system detects a potential deadlock before putting the process to sleep. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 fcntl() section ERRORS

prompt: Does the fstat() function update the st_uid, st_gid, st_size, and st_mode fields when the file descriptor references a shared memory object?
target: Yes. "If fildes references a shared memory object, the implementation shall update in the stat structure pointed to by the buf argument the st_uid, st_gid, st_size, and st_mode fields, and only the S_IRUSR, S_IWUSR, S_IRGRP, S_IWGRP, S_IROTH, and S_IWOTH file permission bits need be valid." This clause explicitly mandates the update of these specific fields for shared memory objects. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 fstat() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: Under what condition does the fstat() function fail due to an I/O error?
target: Yes, the fstat() function fails if an I/O error occurs while reading from the file system. "An I/O error occurred while reading from the file system." This specific error condition is listed under the [EIO] error code in the section text. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 fstat() section ERRORS

prompt: Does the child process inherit file locks set by the parent process after a fork() call?
target: No. "File locks set by the parent process shall not be inherited by the child process." This clause explicitly states that the file locks established by the parent are not carried over to the new child process. Therefore, the child process starts with no inherited file locks from the parent. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 fork() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: Under what condition does the fork() function fail due to the system-imposed limit on the total number of processes?
target: Yes, the fork() function fails if the system-imposed limit on the total number of processes under execution system-wide or by a single user {CHILD_MAX} would be exceeded. "The system lacked the necessary resources to create another process, or the system-imposed limit on the total number of processes under execution system-wide or by a single user {CHILD_MAX} would be exceeded." This means that when the maximum allowed processes are reached, the function cannot create a new process. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 fork() section ERRORS

prompt: Does the exec family of functions preserve alternate signal stacks after a successful call?
target: No. "After a successful call to any of the exec functions, alternate signal stacks are not preserved and the SA_ONSTACK flag shall be cleared for all signals." This means that any alternate signal stacks previously set up are lost, and the SA_ONSTACK flag is reset for all signals in the new process image. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 exec() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: Under what condition does the exec function fail with the error code [E2BIG]?
target: Yes, the exec functions fail with [E2BIG] when the argument and environment lists exceed the system limit. "The number of bytes used by the new process image's argument list and environment list is greater than the system-imposed limit of {ARG_MAX} bytes." This means the system cannot accommodate the new process's data within the defined maximum byte count. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 exec() section ERRORS

prompt: What happens to the status of a child process that terminated normally if the process returned 0 from main()?
target: Yes, the status indicates normal termination with a return value of 0. "The value stored at the location pointed to by stat_loc shall be 0 if and only if the status returned is from a terminated child process that terminated by one of the following means: The process returned 0 from main()." This means that when a child process exits normally by returning 0 from main(), the status value stored at stat_loc will be 0. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 wait() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: What happens to the value of the location pointed to by stat_loc if the wait() function is interrupted by a signal?
target: Yes, the value becomes undefined. "The value of the location pointed to by stat_loc is undefined." This occurs specifically when the function is interrupted by a signal under the [EINTR] error condition. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 wait() section ERRORS

prompt: Under what conditions does the waitpid() function report the status of a continued child process?
target: Yes, the waitpid() function reports the status of a continued child process when the WCONTINUED flag is specified. "The waitpid() function shall report the status of any continued child process specified by pid whose status has not been reported since it continued from a job control stop." This means that if a child process resumes from a job control stop and the WCONTINUED flag is used, the function will specifically report this status if it hasn't been reported before. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 waitpid() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: Does the _Exit() function flush open streams before terminating the process?
target: No. "Open streams shall not be flushed." The text explicitly states that streams are not flushed, though whether they are closed without flushing is implementation-defined. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 _exit() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: Does the kill() function send a signal to the receiving process if the sending process lacks permission and does not have appropriate privileges?
target: No. "For a process to have permission to send a signal to a process designated by pid, unless the sending process has appropriate privileges, the real or effective user ID of the sending process shall match the real or saved set-user-ID of the receiving process." If the user IDs do not match and the sender lacks privileges, permission is not granted, and consequently, no signal is sent. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 kill() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: What condition causes the kill() function to fail if no process or process group corresponds to the specified pid?
target: Yes, the function fails under this condition. "[ESRCH] No process or process group can be found corresponding to that specified by pid." This error code indicates that the target process or group was not found. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 kill() section ERRORS

prompt: Does the pthread_create() function return an error code of [EINTR]?
target: No. "The pthread_create() function shall not return an error code of [EINTR]." Therefore, when a thread is created, the function will never return [EINTR] as an error code. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 pthread_create() section ERRORS

prompt: What happens to the target thread if the calling thread is canceled while waiting for it via pthread_join()?
target: Yes, the target thread remains attached. "If the thread calling pthread_join() is canceled, then the target thread shall not be detached." This means the cancellation of the joining thread does not automatically detach the target thread, leaving it joinable for a future call. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 pthread_join() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: Does the pthread_join() function return an error code of [EINTR]?
target: No. "The pthread_join() function shall not return an error code of [EINTR]." This means that when a thread joins, the function will never return with the specific error code indicating an interrupt. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 pthread_join() section ERRORS

prompt: What happens to the lock count when a thread successfully acquires a PTHREAD_MUTEX_RECURSIVE mutex for the first time?
target: Yes, the lock count is set to one. "When a thread successfully acquires a mutex for the first time, the lock count shall be set to one." This rule applies specifically to recursive mutexes where the count increments on relocking and decrements on unlocking until it reaches zero. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 pthread_mutex_lock() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: Under what condition does the pthread_mutex_lock() function fail with the error code [EDEADLK]?
target: Yes, the function fails with [EDEADLK] when a deadlock condition is detected. "A deadlock condition was detected." This occurs specifically when the pthread_mutex_lock() function is called and the system identifies a potential or actual deadlock. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 pthread_mutex_lock() section ERRORS

prompt: Does the SA_RESTART flag cause an interruptible function to restart and avoid failing with [EINTR] when interrupted by a signal?
target: Yes. "If set, and a function specified as interruptible is interrupted by this signal, the function shall restart and shall not fail with [EINTR] unless otherwise specified." This clause explicitly defines the behavior where the function restarts and does not return the [EINTR] error code. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 sigaction() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: Under what condition does the sigaction() function fail if the SA_SIGINFO flag is set in the sa_flags field for a signal not in the range SIGRTMIN to SIGRTMAX on systems that do not support the XSI option?
target: Yes, the function may fail. "In addition, on systems that do not support the XSI option, the sigaction() function may fail if the SA_SIGINFO flag is set in the sa_flags field of the sigaction structure for a signal not in the range SIGRTMIN to SIGRTMAX." This means that if the system lacks XSI support and the flag is set for a signal outside the real-time range, the function is not guaranteed to succeed. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 sigaction() section ERRORS

prompt: Does the pthread_sigmask() function return an error code of [EINTR]?
target: No. "The pthread_sigmask() function shall not return an error code of [EINTR]." This means the function is guaranteed to complete without returning that specific error code. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 sigprocmask() section ERRORS

prompt: What is the behavior of the signal() function regarding the errno variable if it is successful?
target: Yes, the signal() function does not change the setting of errno if successful. "The signal() function shall not change the setting of errno if successful." This means that upon a successful call, the value of errno remains unchanged, allowing the application to rely on its previous state. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 signal() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: Does the fsync() function guarantee that all currently queued I/O operations are completed when _POSIX_SYNCHRONIZED_IO is defined?
target: Yes. "If _POSIX_SYNCHRONIZED_IO is defined, the fsync() function shall force all currently queued I/O operations associated with the file indicated by file descriptor fildes to the synchronized I/O completion state." This clause explicitly mandates that the function forces queued operations to a synchronized state, ensuring completion as defined for synchronized I/O file integrity. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 fsync() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: What error condition is returned if the fildes argument is not a valid descriptor?
target: Yes, the function fails with [EBADF]. "The fildes argument is not a valid descriptor." This clause explicitly defines the condition for the [EBADF] error. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 fsync() section ERRORS

prompt: Is the functionality of fdatasync() equivalent to fsync() with the symbol _POSIX_SYNCHRONIZED_IO defined, except that all I/O operations shall be completed as defined for synchronized I/O data integrity completion?
target: Yes. "The functionality shall be equivalent to fsync() with the symbol _POSIX_SYNCHRONIZED_IO defined, with the exception that all I/O operations shall be completed as defined for synchronized I/O data integrity completion." This confirms that fdatasync() behaves like fsync() but restricts completion to data integrity rather than full metadata. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 fdatasync() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: What error condition is returned if the fildes argument is not a valid file descriptor?
target: Yes, the function shall fail with [EBADF]. "The fildes argument is not a valid file descriptor." This clause explicitly defines the condition under which the [EBADF] error occurs. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 fdatasync() section ERRORS

prompt: What happens if the ftruncate() function is called on a directory?
target: Yes, the function fails. "If fildes refers to a directory, ftruncate() shall fail." Since the text explicitly states that a directory is a specific case where the function shall fail, the operation will not succeed. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 ftruncate() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: What happens if the length argument provided to ftruncate() is less than 0?
target: Yes, the function shall fail. "[EINVAL] The length argument was less than 0." This means the error code EINVAL is returned when the specified length is negative. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 ftruncate() section ERRORS

prompt: Does the stat() function require read, write, or execute permission of the named file to obtain information about it?
target: No. "Read, write, or execute permission of the named file is not required." This means the function can retrieve file information regardless of the user's access rights to the file itself. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 stat() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: Does the stat function fail if the length of a component of a pathname is longer than {NAME_MAX}?
target: Yes. "The length of a component of a pathname is longer than {NAME_MAX}." This condition is explicitly listed under the [ENAMETOOLONG] error code for the stat functions. Therefore, the function shall fail when this specific length constraint is exceeded. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 stat() section ERRORS

prompt: What happens to the file contents if one or more processes have the file open when the last link is removed?
target: Yes, the removal of the file contents is postponed until all references to the file are closed. "If one or more processes have the file open when the last link is removed, the link shall be removed before unlink() returns, but the removal of the file contents shall be postponed until all references to the file are closed." This means the link is deleted immediately, but the actual file data remains accessible to the open processes until they close the file. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 unlink() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: Does the unlink() function fail if the file named by the path argument is a directory and the implementation prohibits using unlink() on directories?
target: Yes. "[EPERM] The file named by path is a directory, and either the calling process does not have appropriate privileges, or the implementation prohibits using unlink() on directories." This clause explicitly states that the function shall fail under these specific conditions. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 unlink() section ERRORS

prompt: What happens to the file contents if the link named by the new argument exists, the file's link count becomes 0 when it is removed, and no process has the file open?
target: The space occupied by the file shall be freed and the file shall no longer be accessible. "If the link named by the new argument exists and the file's link count becomes 0 when it is removed and no process has the file open, the space occupied by the file shall be freed and the file shall no longer be accessible." This means that once the last link is removed without any open processes, the file is immediately deallocated. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 rename() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: Does the rename() function fail if the directory named by the old argument is currently in use by the system?
target: Yes. "The directory named by old or new is currently in use by the system or another process, and the implementation considers this an error." This condition corresponds to the [EBUSY] error code, indicating that the system treats a directory currently in use as a failure condition for the rename operation. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 rename() section ERRORS

prompt: Does the mmap() function require the file descriptor to be opened with read permission regardless of the protection options specified?
target: Yes. "The file descriptor fildes shall have been opened with read permission, regardless of the protection options specified." This clause explicitly mandates that read permission is a prerequisite for the file descriptor irrespective of whether PROT_READ, PROT_WRITE, or other flags are set. Therefore, the answer is affirmative based on this direct requirement. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 mmap() section DESCRIPTION

prompt: Under what conditions does the mmap() function fail if the fildes argument refers to a file whose type is not supported?
target: Yes, the mmap() function fails if the file type is not supported. "The fildes argument refers to a file whose type is not supported by mmap()." This error is specifically listed under the [ENODEV] condition in the section text. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 mmap() section ERRORS

prompt: Does the sysconf() function support all variables listed in the table provided in the DESCRIPTION section?
target: Yes. "The implementation shall support all of the variables listed in the following table and may support others." This sentence explicitly mandates that the implementation must support every variable shown in the table. Therefore, the function is guaranteed to return values for all listed system variables. Cite: POSIX.1-2017 sysconf() section DESCRIPTION
